Algebra I · Lesson 1.6

Evaluating Expressions

Solve this lesson, free →All lessons

Chapter 1 so far has been about reading. 1.2 fixed the order a computation runs in, 1.4 named the parts of an expression, and 1.5 gave exponents their meaning. This lesson runs the calculation. Pick a value for the variable, substitute it, compute, and a single number comes out.

Problem
Take the expression 7+2n27+2n2 and set n=3n=3. Replace the letter with its number, then follow the order of operations from 1.2. What single value comes out?
Show a hint
  • The exponent applies only to nn, not to 2n2n.
Show the full solution
Substituting gives 7+2(3)2=7+2⋅9=7+18=257+2(3)2=7+2⋅9=7+18=25​. The exponent binds only to nn. Squaring 2n2n instead gives (6)2=36(6)2=36 and the wrong total 4343.
Key idea
Evaluating an expression. To evaluate an expression, replace each variable with its value, then compute by the order of operations from 1.2. The output is a single number. A different value for the variable gives a different output, so a single expression covers infinitely many arithmetic problems, one for each value you choose.
Problem
Now an input with a sign attached. Evaluate 5−x5−x at x=−9x=−9. Two minus signs are in play, one written in the expression and one that is part of the value, and the answer depends on keeping them apart.
Show a hint
  • Write the substitution down on paper before computing anything.
  • What exactly replaces xx, the number 99 or the number −9−9?
Show the full solution
The value of xx is −9−9, sign included, so the expression becomes 5−(−9)5−(−9). Subtracting a negative is adding, as covered in 1.3, so 5+9=145+9=14​. Substituting a bare 99 reads 5−9=−45−9=−4, which is why the parentheses are worth writing.
Key idea
Substitute inside parentheses. When you substitute a value, write it inside parentheses. At x=−9x=−9, the expression 5−x5−x becomes 5−(−9)5−(−9), never a bare 5−95−9. Parentheses are needed because the minus sign in the expression and the minus sign that is part of the value are two different signs. Without them the two read as one sign.
Problem
Evaluate 3x23x2 at x=−5x=−5. Decide two things before you compute, what exactly the exponent touches, and what squaring does to the sign of the value.
Show a hint
  • The exponent binds only to xx, not to 3x3x. That reading came from 1.2.
  • The value of xx is −5−5, all of it, so the parentheses habit puts the whole thing under the square.
Show the full solution
Only xx is squared, and xx is −5−5 with its sign, so 3(−5)2=3⋅25=753(−5)2=3⋅25=75​. Squaring the product would give (−15)2=225(−15)2=225, and reading the square as −52=−(52)−52=−(52) would give −75−75.
Key idea
Exponents under substitution. x2x2 at x=−5x=−5 means (−5)2=25(−5)2=25, because xx stands for the whole value, sign included, and squaring multiplies that whole value by itself. Skip the parentheses and the line reads −52−52, which by 1.2 means −(52)=−25−(52)=−25, a different and wrong number. Write the parentheses every time.
Problem
The letter ww appears twice in w(w−5)w(w−5). Evaluate it at w=8w=8. Both appearances take the value at the same moment, and the parentheses still group exactly as they did in 1.2.
Show a hint
  • Substitute 88 at both spots first, then finish inside the parentheses before multiplying.
Show the full solution
Both wws become 88, so the expression reads 8(8−5)8(8−5). The parentheses finish first, and 8⋅3=248⋅3=24​. Reading it as 8⋅8−5=598⋅8−5=59 drops the grouping.
Key idea
One letter, one value. Within a single evaluation, the same letter means the same number at every appearance, so both wws in w(w−5)w(w−5) become 88. Each different letter has its own value. Substitute first, then do the arithmetic. Once every letter is replaced, what remains is a 1.2 arithmetic problem.
Problem
Two letters, two values, four sign decisions. Evaluate 2x−3y2x−3y at x=−1x=−1 and y=−4y=−4, writing each substituted value inside its own parentheses before computing anything.
Show a hint
  • After substituting, the line reads 2(−1)−3(−4)2(−1)−3(−4), and the middle minus applies to the whole product 3(−4)3(−4).
Show the full solution
Substituting gives 2(−1)−3(−4)2(−1)−3(−4). The products are −2−2 and −12−12, and subtracting −12−12 is adding 1212, so −2+12=10−2+12=10​. Losing the second sign gives −2−12=−14−2−12=−14.
Problem
Evaluate m+14m−2m−2m+14​ at m=6m=6. Typed on one line as m+14/m−2m+14/m−2, the expression loses its grouping, so work it as written, with the whole top as one computation and the whole bottom as another.
Show a hint
  • The fraction bar wraps everything above it and everything below it, the invisible grouping from 1.2.
Show the full solution
The top is 6+14=206+14=20, the bottom is 6−2=46−2=4, and 20÷4=520÷4=5​. The bar groups the whole top and the whole bottom. Collapsed onto one line without parentheses, that grouping is lost and the pieces combine in the wrong order.
Key idea
Substitution keeps the grouping. A fraction bar groups its entire top and its entire bottom, the invisible grouping from 1.2. Substituting values does not change that, because the grouping belongs to the expression and not to the letters. Finish the whole top, finish the whole bottom, and divide last. A radical bar works the same way, grouping everything under it before the root is taken.
Problem
Nothing about substitution needs whole numbers. Evaluate 8g2+g8g2+g at g=12g=21​. The exponent question comes first, what (12)2(21​)2 is, and 1.5 already answered it. Enter the value as a fraction in lowest terms.
Show a hint
  • Squaring 1221​ makes it smaller, not the same and not doubled.
Show the full solution
Squaring gives (12)2=14(21​)2=41​, so 8⋅14=28⋅41​=2, and 2+12=522+21​=25​​. Squaring a fraction below 11 makes it smaller. Treating the square as 1221​ would give 9229​.
Problem
Formulas are expressions somebody already built for you. A dropped object falls 16t216t2 feet in its first tt seconds. Evaluate the expression at t=3t=3 to find how far, in feet, the object falls in three seconds.
Show a hint
  • The exponent binds only to tt, so square first, then multiply by 1616.
Show the full solution
Square first, 32=932=9, then 16⋅9=14416⋅9=144​ feet. The exponent binds only to tt. Applying it to the whole product gives (16⋅3)2=2304(16⋅3)2=2304, which misreads the formula.
Key idea
Formulas. A formula is an expression someone already wrote and named. Physics and geometry are full of them. Using one is exactly this lesson. Substitute the given values, follow the order of operations, read off the number. The reading rules do not change just because an expression has a name, so the exponent in 16t216t2 still binds only to tt, and 16(3)216(3)2 means 16⋅916⋅9, never (16⋅3)2(16⋅3)2.
Problem
Everything in this lesson at once. Evaluate x2−5xx+1x+1x2−5x​ at x=−3x=−3. Substitute in parentheses at every appearance, finish the top and the bottom separately, and divide last.
Show a hint
  • Three appearances of xx means three sets of parentheses.
  • Both terms on top come out positive.
Show the full solution
The top is (−3)2−5(−3)=9+15=24(−3)2−5(−3)=9+15=24, the bottom is −3+1=−2−3+1=−2, and 24÷(−2)=−1224÷(−2)=−12​. Both wrong routes are sign slips, reading x2x2 as −32=−9−32=−9, or losing the sign in −5(−3)−5(−3). Parentheses at every appearance shut both down.
Fun fact
Every spreadsheet cell that holds a formula, and every frame of every video game, is a computer doing exactly this, substituting the current values into an expression and computing by the same order of operations you use by hand.

That closes Chapter 1. You can read any expression the way its writer meant it, name its variables, terms, coefficients, and factors, and unwind its exponents. You can also evaluate it at any input, whole, negative, or fractional. Chapter 2 rewrites expressions into simpler forms, and it opens with the distributive property in 2.1.

Practice these ideas

Practice
Evaluate 4n+94n+9 at n=5n=5.
Show the solution
Substituting gives 4(5)+94(5)+9. Adding first reads 5+9=145+9=14 and computes 4⋅14=564⋅14=56, but the product finishes before the sum, so 4⋅5=204⋅5=20 and 20+9=2920+9=29​.
Practice
Evaluate 30−2k30−2k at k=6k=6. By the 1.2 order the product finishes before the subtraction.
Show the solution
Working left to right reads 30−2=2830−2=28 and then multiplies by 66, which misorders the steps. The product goes first, so 30−12=1830−12=18​.
Practice
Evaluate y2−yy2−y at y=9y=9. Both appearances of yy take the same value, and the exponent goes first.
Show the solution
Both appearances become 99 at the same moment, so the expression reads 92−992−9. The tempting slip is to subtract first and then square, which would give (9−9)2=0(9−9)2=0. The exponent finishes before the subtraction, so 81−9=7281−9=72​.
Practice
Evaluate 7−w7−w at w=−8w=−8. Write the value inside parentheses, sign included, before computing anything.
Show the solution
The careless route reads 7−8=−17−8=−1, which substitutes 88 and drops the sign that belongs to the value. Written as 7−(−8)7−(−8) it is 7+8=157+8=15​.
Practice
Evaluate −t−t at t=−12t=−12. With the habit the substitution reads −(−12)−(−12), the opposite of a negative.
Show the solution
The tempting answer is −12−12, keeping the value itself. The minus written in −t−t is not part of the value, it asks for the opposite of tt, and the opposite of −12−12 is 1212​.
Practice
Evaluate 5x25x2 at x=−2x=−2. Decide exactly what the exponent touches before you multiply.
Show the solution
There are two wrong turns, squaring the product to get (−10)2=100(−10)2=100, and reading the square as −22=−4−22=−4 to get −20−20. The exponent binds only to xx, and xx is −2−2 with its sign, so 5(−2)2=5⋅4=205(−2)2=5⋅4=20​.
Practice
Evaluate 4a−5b4a−5b at a=3a=3 and b=−2b=−2. Substitute both values before simplifying.
Show the solution
Losing the sign on bb reads the second term as 5⋅25⋅2 and gives 12−10=212−10=2. With parentheses the substitution is 4(3)−5(−2)=12+10=224(3)−5(−2)=12+10=22​.
Practice
Evaluate p+11p−4p−4p+11​ at p=9p=9. Finish the whole top and the whole bottom, then divide.
Show the solution
Collapsed onto one line the bar's grouping is lost and the pieces combine in the wrong order. The top is 9+11=209+11=20 and the bottom is 9−4=59−4=5, each finished on its own before any dividing. Then 20÷5=420÷5=4​.
Practice
Evaluate 6q26q2 at q=12q=21​. Enter the value as a fraction in lowest terms.
Show the solution
Treating the square of 1221​ as 1221​ gives 33, wrong. Squaring makes it smaller, (12)2=14(21​)2=41​, so the value is 6⋅14=326⋅41​=23​​.
Practice
The expression 6s26s2 gives the surface area of a cube with side length ss, six square faces of area s2s2 each. Evaluate it at s=4s=4.
Show the solution
The tempting slip squares the product, (6⋅4)2=576(6⋅4)2=576. The exponent binds only to ss, so 6(4)2=6⋅16=966(4)2=6⋅16=96​.
Practice
Evaluate u2+3uu+9u+9u2+3u​ at u=−4u=−4. Parentheses at every substitution. Enter the value as a fraction in lowest terms.
Show the solution
Reading the square as −42=−16−42=−16 makes the top −28−28 and everything after it wrong. The correct top is (−4)2+3(−4)=16−12=4(−4)2+3(−4)=16−12=4 over a bottom of −4+9=5−4+9=5, so the value is 4554​​.
Practice
At n=1,2,3,4n=1,2,3,4 the expression n2−n+17n2−n+17 gives 17, 19, 23, 2917, 19, 23, 29, a prime every time, and the streak continues for many inputs after that. It is tempting to conclude it always gives a prime. Evaluate it at n=17n=17, then look hard at the output.
Show the solution
Running the recipe gives 172−17+17=289172−17+17=289, and 289=17⋅17289=17⋅17, which is not prime, so the pattern breaks at the seventeenth input. Sixteen prime outputs in a row never proved the claim, and one counterexample settles it, the same point 1.4 made about checking values. The output is 289289​.
